title: Born in Duluth, Minnesota
text: Robert Allen Zimmerman was born on May 24, 1941, in Duluth, Minnesota, to Abram and Beatty Zimmerman.
long: Duluth is a port city at the western tip of Lake Superior, and his parents belonged to its small Jewish community; his father Abram worked for Standard Oil there. The boy spent only his first few years in the city before the family moved inland to the Iron Range, so most of what later shaped him came from Hibbing rather than the harbor town. Duluth still turns up in his story. In his Nobel lecture he recalled seeing Buddy Holly play the Duluth Armory in early 1959, just days before Holly died, and described that show as a turning point for him. Decades later the city began marking its connection to him, and the house where he spent his earliest years still stands on a hillside above the lake.

title: Family moves to Hibbing
text: After his father fell ill with polio, the family moved to Hibbing, an iron-range mining town where Beatty's family lived.
long: Abram Zimmerman's illness ended his job in Duluth, and in Hibbing he went into business with his brothers, running a furniture and appliance store. Hibbing was built around one of the largest open-pit iron mines in the world, a cold, working town far from any music industry. That distance mattered. Late at night the boy listened to faraway radio stations that carried country, blues and early rhythm and blues, and Hank Williams became one of his first heroes. He had a younger brother, David, and a fairly ordinary small-town childhood, including his bar mitzvah in 1954. Years later he would speak of the town with mixed feelings, but the landscape and the sense of isolation stayed with him and surface again and again in his songs about the North Country.

title: Graduates from Hibbing High School
text: After years of playing rock and roll in school bands, he graduated from Hibbing High School in 1959.
long: By his teens he was banging out Little Richard numbers on the piano and leading a string of short-lived school bands, among them the Golden Chords. At least one talent-show performance was loud enough that the school cut it short, a story classmates told for years afterwards. He also had a high school girlfriend, Echo Helstrom, often named as an inspiration for his later song "Girl from the North Country". Rock and roll, more than folk music, was his passion at this point, and he dreamed of the kind of stardom Elvis Presley had. Graduation meant leaving Hibbing. That summer he briefly played piano with Bobby Vee's band in Fargo, and in the autumn he moved south to Minneapolis, where his musical direction would change quickly.

title: University of Minnesota and Dinkytown
text: He enrolled at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis, where he immersed himself in the Dinkytown folk scene and began performing as Bob Dylan.
long: Dinkytown was the bohemian neighborhood next to the campus, full of coffeehouses, bookshops and student apartments. There he traded rock and roll for acoustic folk music, learning old ballads and blues from records borrowed from friends and playing for small change at places like the Ten O'Clock Scholar. Reading Woody Guthrie's autobiography, Bound for Glory, and hearing his records changed everything: he began to dress, talk and sing in Guthrie's style. He spent little time on his studies and drifted away from the university within about a year. The new name stuck, and so did his ambition. Near the end of 1960 he decided that Minneapolis was too small, and he set out for New York, where the folk revival was at its center and where he hoped to meet Guthrie himself.

title: Arrives in New York and visits Woody Guthrie
text: Dylan reached New York in January 1961 and soon visited his hero Woody Guthrie, hospitalized with Huntington's disease in New Jersey, while playing Greenwich Village coffeehouses.
long: He arrived in the middle of a hard winter and found his way to Greenwich Village, where he played for tips at the Cafe Wha? and other clubs and slept on friends' couches. Guthrie, his idol, was by then too ill to perform, living in Greystone Park Psychiatric Hospital in New Jersey. Dylan visited him there, played him songs and also called on him at the home of friends who hosted Guthrie on Sundays. Out of those visits came "Song to Woody", one of the first strong songs he wrote, a tribute that later appeared on his debut album. The encounters gave the newcomer a direct link to the folk tradition he admired, and within months he had become a familiar figure on the Village scene, learning from older singers such as Dave Van Ronk.

title: New York Times review and Columbia contract
text: Robert Shelton's glowing New York Times review of Dylan's show at Gerde's Folk City appeared in September 1961, and John Hammond signed him to Columbia Records soon after.
long: Dylan was opening for the bluegrass group the Greenbriar Boys at Gerde's, but Shelton's review gave the young unknown most of the attention, praising his originality and his rough charm. Around the same time he played harmonica on a recording session for the singer Carolyn Hester, where the veteran producer John Hammond noticed him. Hammond offered him a contract with Columbia, an unusual move for a major label with a scruffy folk singer, and some at the company doubted the decision. His first album, Bob Dylan, was recorded quickly in late 1961 and came out in 1962. It consisted mostly of traditional songs and blues, with only two originals, and sold modestly. Shelton remained a supporter and later wrote a full biography of him.

title: Newport Folk Festival 1963
text: At his first Newport Folk Festival in July 1963 Dylan sang with Joan Baez, and the festival closed with performers joining hands for "Blowin' in the Wind" and "We Shall Overcome".
long: Newport was the most important gathering of the folk revival, and in 1963 Dylan arrived there as its rising star. His second album, The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan, had come out that spring, and Peter, Paul and Mary had turned "Blowin' in the Wind" into a hit. Joan Baez, already famous, brought him on stage with her and championed his songs, and the two became a public pairing. The closing scene, with the Freedom Singers, Pete Seeger, Baez and others singing together, tied his music to the civil rights movement in the public mind. Baez soon invited him on her own tour as a guest, introducing him to larger audiences. He returned to Newport in 1964 and again in 1965, when his appearance would go very differently.

title: March on Washington
text: On August 28, 1963, Dylan performed at the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, including "Only a Pawn in Their Game".
long: The march drew a vast crowd to the Lincoln Memorial, and the musical program included Joan Baez, Odetta, Mahalia Jackson and Peter, Paul and Mary. Dylan's song was about the murder of the civil rights leader Medgar Evers in Mississippi earlier that summer, and it argued that the man who pulled the trigger was a tool of politicians who stirred up racial hatred. He also sang "When the Ship Comes In" with Baez. Later that afternoon Martin Luther King Jr. gave his famous speech. The day sealed his image as a voice of the movement, an image he soon found confining. Within a year he was writing more personal songs, and Another Side of Bob Dylan, released in 1964, moved away from topical protest.

title: Solo tour of England, filmed for Dont Look Back
text: In the spring of 1965 Dylan toured England with an acoustic show, and D. A. Pennebaker filmed the trip for the documentary Dont Look Back, released in 1967.
long: The tour came just after Bringing It All Back Home, an album with one electric side and one acoustic side, yet on stage he still appeared alone with guitar and harmonica. British fans treated him as a star, and the press followed him everywhere. Pennebaker's camera caught the backstage life: sparring with reporters, hotel-room song swaps, Joan Baez in the entourage, a meeting with Donovan, and his manager Albert Grossman at work. The film's opening, with Dylan flipping cue cards to "Subterranean Homesick Blues", became one of the most imitated images in music. It was the last tour of his solo acoustic period. Weeks after returning home he recorded "Like a Rolling Stone", and the sound of his music changed for good.

title: Newport Folk Festival: plays electric
text: On July 25, 1965, Dylan took the Newport stage backed by members of the Paul Butterfield Blues Band, and his short, loud electric set drew boos from part of the folk crowd.
long: Newport had celebrated him as a folk hero, so the change was startling. With Mike Bloomfield on guitar, Al Kooper on organ and a rhythm section from the Butterfield band, he played only three songs, including "Maggie's Farm" and the newly released "Like a Rolling Stone". Some of the crowd jeered; how many, and whether at the music, the poor sound or the short set, has been argued about ever since. He came back alone with an acoustic guitar for two more songs. The night became the best-known symbol of folk music meeting rock. Highway 61 Revisited followed within weeks, and he soon went on tour with the Hawks, facing similar hostility. The 2024 film A Complete Unknown ends with this night.

title: Marries Sara Lownds
text: In November 1965 Dylan quietly married Sara Lownds, a former model, in a private ceremony on Long Island.
long: Sara had a young daughter, Maria, from her first marriage, whom Dylan later adopted. The wedding was kept so quiet that the press did not learn of it for months. The couple had four more children together, including Jesse, born in early 1966, and Jakob, who later led the band the Wallflowers. After the frenzy of 1965 and 1966 they settled into family life in Woodstock, and he largely kept his private life out of view. Many listeners connect "Sad Eyed Lady of the Lowlands", the long closing song of Blonde on Blonde, with her, and he later wrote "Sara" for Desire. The marriage ran into trouble in the mid 1970s, and they divorced in 1977.

title: Motorcycle accident near Woodstock
text: In late July 1966 Dylan crashed his Triumph motorcycle near his home in Woodstock, New York, and afterwards stopped touring for years.
long: The crash came at the end of an exhausting stretch of recording and touring, with more concerts already booked. How badly he was hurt has never been fully clear; no detailed medical account was made public, and he recovered privately, partly at the home of a doctor in Middletown, New York. Whatever the injuries, the accident gave him a reason to stop. He cancelled his upcoming shows, spent time with his growing family and stayed out of public view. In that quiet he made the basement recordings with the Hawks and then John Wesley Harding, a spare, restrained record very unlike his mid-1960s sound. Apart from a handful of one-off appearances, he did not tour again until 1974, and the accident has fed his legend ever since.

title: "Judas!" at the Manchester Free Trade Hall
text: On May 17, 1966, during his world tour with the Hawks, an audience member in Manchester shouted "Judas" at Dylan during the electric half of the show.
long: On that 1966 tour each concert had two halves: a quiet acoustic set, then a loud one with the Hawks, and many folk fans booed the second half night after night. In Manchester a voice from the audience called him a traitor in the harshest terms. Dylan answered that he did not believe him and called him a liar, then turned to the band and told them to play loud before launching into "Like a Rolling Stone". The recording circulated for decades on bootlegs mislabeled as the Royal Albert Hall concert. Columbia officially released it in 1998 as Live 1966, part of the Bootleg Series, and it is now regarded as one of the great live rock recordings. More than one man has since claimed to be the heckler.

title: Woodstock: basement sessions with the Hawks
text: Through 1967 Dylan recorded dozens of informal songs with members of the Hawks, soon to be the Band, in the basement of a house called Big Pink near Woodstock.
long: The sessions were relaxed and unplanned. Garth Hudson ran a tape recorder while the group worked through old folk ballads, country songs and blues alongside a stream of new Dylan songs, some funny, some strange, some deeply serious, among them "I Shall Be Released" and "This Wheel's on Fire". Demo tapes went to his music publisher, and other artists such as Manfred Mann and the Byrds had hits with the songs. A bootleg called Great White Wonder appeared in 1969, one of the first rock bootlegs. Columbia issued a selection as The Basement Tapes in 1975 and a near-complete set in 2014. The Band's own debut, Music from Big Pink, came out in 1968, and the sessions helped shape the rootsier sound of the late 1960s.

title: Isle of Wight Festival
text: On August 31, 1969, backed by the Band, he headlined the Isle of Wight Festival in England, his first full-length concert since 1966.
long: He had turned down the chance to play Woodstock, near his own home, a few weeks earlier, so the British show carried huge expectations. A very large crowd came, and members of the Beatles were among those who watched. He performed for about an hour, dressed in a white suit, singing in the softer, smoother voice of his recent Nashville Skyline and reworking older songs in country style. Some critics and fans who had waited years were disappointed by the short, mellow set; others found it warm and relaxed. A few of the performances appeared on Self Portrait in 1970, and the full concert was released decades later as part of the Bootleg Series. It was his last major concert before the Band tour of 1974.

title: Honorary doctorate from Princeton
text: In June 1970 Princeton University gave him an honorary Doctor of Music degree, a day he later turned into a song on New Morning.
long: He went to the ceremony reluctantly, accompanied by his wife Sara and David Crosby, and found the formality uncomfortable. It was a hot day, and the air was full of the noise of cicadas emerging that summer. He wrote about the experience as "Day of the Locusts", released on New Morning later in 1970, and recalled it again in his memoir Chronicles, Volume One. The degree was an early sign that the academic world took him seriously as a writer, at a time when his new records were getting mixed reviews. Far larger honors came later: a special Pulitzer citation in 2008, the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012 and the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2016.

title: Acts in Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid
text: Dylan took a small role as a character called Alias in Sam Peckinpah's western, filmed in Mexico, and wrote its score.
long: The film starred James Coburn as Pat Garrett and Kris Kristofferson as Billy the Kid, and was shot in Durango, Mexico, in a production troubled by clashes between Peckinpah and the studio. Dylan's part was small and enigmatic, a drifter who attaches himself to Billy's gang. His music did more. The soundtrack album, released in 1973, is mostly instrumental, but it includes "Knockin' on Heaven's Door", which became a hit and one of his most covered songs, later recorded by Eric Clapton and Guns N' Roses among many others. MGM released a cut version of the film that Peckinpah disowned, and fuller versions appeared later. Soon after, Dylan left Columbia for a time and signed with Asylum Records.

title: Back on the road with the Band
text: In January and February 1974 he toured North American arenas with the Band, his first full tour since 1966, captured on the live album Before the Flood.
long: The tour was promoted by Bill Graham, and demand for tickets was enormous, with millions of mail-order requests for the available seats. It followed the release of Planet Waves, recorded with the Band and issued on Asylum, his first studio album with them. On stage the music was loud and urgent, with Dylan pushing his older songs hard and the Band playing sets of their own between his. Before the Flood, drawn largely from the final shows in Los Angeles, came out later in 1974. The tour proved he could still fill arenas after eight years away. Before the year was out he had returned to Columbia and recorded Blood on the Tracks, often counted among his finest albums.

title: The Rolling Thunder Revue
text: Starting in Plymouth, Massachusetts in October 1975, he led a travelling caravan of musicians including Joan Baez and Roger McGuinn at first through smaller halls in New England and Canada.
long: The revue was loose and theatrical. Alongside Baez and McGuinn came Bob Neuwirth, Ramblin' Jack Elliott, Mick Ronson, violinist Scarlet Rivera and the poet Allen Ginsberg, with Joni Mitchell joining partway. Dylan often performed in white face paint, and the shows mixed old songs with new ones from Desire, which came out in early 1976. The playwright Sam Shepard traveled along to help with a film, which became Renaldo and Clara, released in 1978. The first leg ended with a benefit for the imprisoned boxer Rubin Carter at Madison Square Garden. A second leg in 1976 produced the album Hard Rain and a television special, and in 2019 Martin Scorsese made a playful documentary about the tour.

title: 1978 world tour
text: He spent most of 1978 touring Japan, Australia, Europe and North America with a large band and backing singers, recording the live album At Budokan in Tokyo.
long: The tour began in Japan early in the year and ran for most of the next ten months, ending in the United States in December. Dylan reworked his old songs with a big band that included saxophone and a trio of women singers, giving many of them new arrangements, sometimes almost unrecognizable. In the middle of the year he released Street-Legal. European audiences responded warmly, including a very large outdoor show at Blackbushe in England, while some American critics mocked the glossy sound as showbusiness. At Budokan, recorded in Tokyo, was issued first in Japan and then worldwide. Near the end of the tour he went through a religious conversion, and by early 1979 he had become a born-again Christian.

title: Saturday Night Live: three gospel songs
text: On October 20, 1979, he played three songs from Slow Train Coming as the musical guest on Saturday Night Live.
long: He played "Gotta Serve Somebody", "I Believe in You" and "When You Gonna Wake Up", all from Slow Train Coming, the album he had made in Muscle Shoals, Alabama, with producers Jerry Wexler and Barry Beckett and Mark Knopfler on guitar. Backed by a tight band and gospel singers, he left no doubt that his new Christian faith was the subject of his music now. For a television audience used to the older Dylan, it was a striking statement. About two weeks later he began a run of shows in San Francisco where he played only his new religious songs, to some boos and walkouts. "Gotta Serve Somebody" went on to win him a Grammy, and the gospel period continued with Saved in 1980.

title: Gospel-only shows at the Warfield
text: Starting November 1, 1979, he played a run of concerts at San Francisco's Fox Warfield Theatre made up only of new religious songs and none of his older hits.
long: The run came a few months after Slow Train Coming, the album that announced his conversion to evangelical Christianity. Fans who bought tickets expecting the familiar songs heard none of them. Instead he fronted a band with a group of gospel backing singers and performed the new religious material, along with songs that would turn up on his next album, Saved, and on some nights he spoke to the crowd about his faith between numbers. Some in the audience booed or walked out, and several reviews were openly hostile. He did not bend. The gospel-only format carried on through the touring that followed into 1980, and for a while it was the only version of Dylan on offer. Whatever people made of the message, the shows held some of the most fervent singing of his career.

title: Grammy for Gotta Serve Somebody
text: In February 1980 he won the Grammy for Best Rock Vocal Performance, Male, for Gotta Serve Somebody and performed the song at the ceremony.
long: The award went to the lead single from Slow Train Coming, the first record of his gospel period. It was a striking piece of mainstream approval at a moment when many longtime listeners were confused or put off by his new direction. At the ceremony he performed the song with his touring band and backing singers, carrying its religious message to a national television audience. The song had also provoked John Lennon, who recorded a mocking home demo in reply. The win suggested the gospel records could still reach a broad public, even as the next album, Saved, met a cooler reception later that year. It remains one of the clearest signs of how seriously the music business took this chapter while it was happening, whatever critics would later decide about it.

title: Older songs return to the set
text: In November 1980 he returned to the Warfield for shows that brought some of his older songs back alongside the gospel material.
long: A year after the gospel-only concerts, he came back to the same San Francisco theater with a different idea of what a show could hold. The religious songs were still there, but now they shared the stage with older material, some of it rearranged, and with new songs pointing toward his next record. Guests sat in on several nights; one was Mike Bloomfield, the guitarist from his 1965 electric sessions, who joined him for a couple of songs only months before his own death. The change showed that the strictest phase of his gospel years was easing. The album that followed in 1981, Shot of Love, mixed faith with other subjects, and from then on his concerts drew freely on every part of his catalog again.

title: Live Aid: closes the Philadelphia show
text: On July 13, 1985, Dylan played near the end of the Live Aid concert at JFK Stadium in Philadelphia, backed by Keith Richards and Ronnie Wood.
long: Live Aid was a two-continent benefit for famine relief in Ethiopia, broadcast around the world from London and Philadelphia. Dylan was placed near the end of the American show, playing acoustic guitar with Richards and Wood beside him. The set was rough: the three could barely hear themselves while preparations for the finale went on behind the curtain, and guitar strings gave trouble. Many viewers remembered it as a ragged moment on a huge stage. Yet one passing remark mattered more than the music. He suggested from the stage that some of the money might help American farmers losing their land to debt. Willie Nelson, Neil Young and John Mellencamp took up the idea, and the first Farm Aid concert was held that September, an event that has continued ever since.

title: Inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame
text: Dylan was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in January 1988, with Bruce Springsteen giving the induction speech.
long: He entered the Hall in only its third year of inductions, in a class that also included the Beatles, the Beach Boys, the Drifters and the Supremes. Springsteen's speech became one of the best remembered in the institution's history. He described first hearing Dylan on the radio as a teenager and how it changed his sense of what a rock record could say, and he credited Dylan with freeing the minds of a generation of songwriters. Dylan's own remarks were brief and wry. The honor arrived at an odd point in his career, after a run of records that had drawn mixed reviews. Within months he would start the touring that defined his later decades and join the Traveling Wilburys, and the following year Oh Mercy would restore much of his critical standing.

title: The Never Ending Tour begins
text: On June 7, 1988, in Concord, California, Dylan began the run of near-continuous touring that fans came to call the Never Ending Tour.
long: After big stadium tours with Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers and with the Grateful Dead, he cut his live show down to a small, hard-hitting band led by guitarist G.E. Smith and started playing far more often. The idea was to treat performing as steady work rather than as a special event, and to keep the songs alive by changing them night after night. The name came from an interview the following year, and Dylan himself never much liked it, but it stuck. For years he played around a hundred shows annually or more, reshaping arrangements, swapping musicians, and moving through theaters, arenas, festivals and minor-league ballparks. The road became the center of his working life, and for many listeners the concerts, more than any album, became the place to hear where he was going next.

title: The Traveling Wilburys
text: Dylan joined George Harrison, Jeff Lynne, Roy Orbison and Tom Petty in the Traveling Wilburys, whose first album came out in October 1988.
long: The group began almost by accident. Harrison needed an extra track for a single and gathered friends to record it, using a studio at Dylan's home in Malibu. The result, "Handle with Care", was too good to tuck away, so the five agreed to make a whole album together under joking pseudonyms as brothers of a fictional Wilbury family. The record, recorded quickly and loosely, had the warm, easy sound of friends trading verses, with each member taking turns at lead vocals. It became a big hit and won a Grammy. Orbison died that December, only weeks after its release. The remaining four made a second album in 1990, wryly titled Vol. 3, and the project gave Dylan a rare taste of being one voice in a band.

title: 30th anniversary concert at Madison Square Garden
text: On October 16, 1992, a host of artists performed his songs at Madison Square Garden to mark thirty years since his first album, and Dylan closed the night himself.
long: Neil Young nicknamed the night Bobfest, and the name stuck. The bill was enormous: Stevie Wonder, Lou Reed, Johnny Cash, Eric Clapton, George Harrison, Tom Petty, Roger McGuinn and Young himself were among those who sang his songs, with Booker T. and the MG's as the house band. The evening is also remembered for Sinéad O'Connor, who was booed so loudly, weeks after a televised protest against the pope, that she abandoned her planned song. Dylan came out at the end, played alone for a few songs, then led an all-star group through a couple of his classics. The concert was released as an album and video the following year. Its broad roster showed how deeply his songs had spread through every corner of popular music over three decades.

title: Sings at the Clinton inaugural celebration
text: In January 1993 Dylan performed Chimes of Freedom at a concert at the Lincoln Memorial celebrating Bill Clinton's inauguration.
long: The concert at the Lincoln Memorial was a public celebration held in the days before Clinton took office, with a long list of performers. Dylan chose "Chimes of Freedom", a song from 1964, rather than one of his better known anthems. Clinton was the first president to come of age in the rock era, and the song's vision of freedom fit the evening's theme of a new generation taking charge. For Dylan, who had spent decades refusing the role of spokesman for anything, it was a rare appearance at an official political occasion. It also showed how far his early songs had moved from protest folk to national heritage. He returned to the White House years later, performing at a 2010 concert honoring the music of the civil rights movement.

title: Album of the Year Grammy for Time Out of Mind
text: In February 1998 Time Out of Mind won the Grammy for Album of the Year, along with two other awards that night.
long: Time Out of Mind, made with producer Daniel Lanois, had come out the previous autumn to the strongest reviews he had received in decades. Its release followed closely on a serious illness in 1997, a heart infection that put him in hospital, and the album's dark, weary atmosphere was widely read in that light. Besides Album of the Year it took Best Contemporary Folk Album, and "Cold Irons Bound" won a rock vocal award. The ceremony is also remembered for a stranger moment: during his performance of "Love Sick", a man with words scrawled on his bare chest jumped beside him and danced until he was led away, while Dylan kept playing. The awards confirmed a late-career revival that his next records would build on.

title: Academy Award for Things Have Changed
text: Dylan won the Oscar for Best Original Song for Things Have Changed, written for the film Wonder Boys; it also took the Golden Globe.
long: Curtis Hanson's film Wonder Boys starred Michael Douglas as a stalled novelist and teacher, and Dylan wrote the song to suit its rueful, worn-out mood. The track pairs a loping groove with a narrator who sounds detached and slightly amused by his own decline, close in spirit to the voice of Time Out of Mind. When the Oscar was awarded in 2001 he was on tour in Australia, so he performed the song by satellite link from there. Afterward he kept the statuette with him on the road and often placed it on an amplifier or the stage, a small joke repeated night after night. The award brought his writing to a wide new audience and set the stage for the album that followed later that year, Love and Theft.

title: Chronicles: Volume One published
text: Dylan's memoir Chronicles: Volume One came out in October 2004 and became a bestseller praised by critics.
long: Instead of a straight life story, the book jumps between a few chosen periods. It spends long stretches on his arrival in New York in the early 1960s, on the folk scene, the clubs and the people who taught him; then turns to a family-centered stretch around 1970 when he tried to escape the role others assigned him; and to the making of Oh Mercy in New Orleans with Daniel Lanois at the end of the 1980s. The writing is vivid, funny and often unexpected, full of portraits of musicians and books that shaped him. Readers who had expected evasions found a generous, detailed storyteller. It was billed as the first of several volumes, but no second volume has followed, and his next major book came nearly two decades later.

title: Presidential Medal of Freedom
text: President Barack Obama awarded Dylan the Presidential Medal of Freedom at the White House in May 2012.
long: The Medal of Freedom is the highest civilian honor in the United States. Dylan received it in the same ceremony as a varied group of others, among them the novelist Toni Morrison, the astronaut and senator John Glenn, and former Secretary of State Madeleine Albright. Obama spoke of being a fan and of what Dylan's music had meant to him as a young man, and Dylan, wearing dark glasses, accepted the medal quietly. The honor followed other official recognitions, including a special Pulitzer Prize citation in 2008, and came two years after he had played at the White House in a concert celebrating the music of the civil rights movement. It placed his songs firmly among American cultural achievements several years before the Nobel committee did the same on an international stage.

title: MusiCares Person of the Year
text: Honored by MusiCares in Los Angeles, he gave a long, rare speech about his songwriting and his critics.
long: MusiCares, the charity linked to the Grammys that helps musicians in need, chose him as its honoree, and a lineup of artists performed his songs at a benefit dinner. Then he took the stage with a prepared text and spoke for around half an hour, an extraordinary length for a man known for terse public remarks. He traced his songs back to the folk, blues and country music he had absorbed when young, explaining how old forms had fed his writing. He thanked the people who had helped him early on, and he also hit back at critics who had complained about his voice for decades, and at a few fellow musicians he felt had slighted him. The speech was widely published afterward and remains one of the clearest accounts he has given of how he works.

title: Nobel Prize in Literature
text: The Swedish Academy named him the 2016 laureate for creating new poetic expressions within the great American song tradition, making him the first songwriter to receive it.
long: The announcement in October set off a debate about whether songs belonged in a literary prize, and Dylan made it stranger by staying silent for about two weeks; one academy member publicly called that silence rude. He eventually said he was honored but did not travel to the December ceremony in Stockholm, citing other commitments. Patti Smith sang "A Hard Rain's A-Gonna Fall" in his place, pausing emotionally partway through, and a short speech he had written was read at the banquet. He accepted the medal and diploma privately in Stockholm the following spring, while on tour. To collect the prize money he still had to deliver a lecture, which he did that June. The award placed him in a line of writers stretching back over a century.

title: Nobel lecture
text: He met the Nobel requirement in June 2017 by sending a recorded lecture on the books and songs that shaped him.
long: The academy's rules required a lecture within six months of the December ceremony, and he sent his as an audio recording, read over a quiet piano. He began with the music that first stirred him, recalling seeing Buddy Holly perform shortly before Holly's death and discovering Lead Belly and the folk tradition. Then he turned to three books from his school years that had stayed with him: Moby-Dick, All Quiet on the Western Front and The Odyssey, retelling each in his own way. He ended by arguing that songs are meant to be sung and heard, not just read on a page. Some writers later pointed to close similarities between parts of his Moby-Dick passage and an online study guide, adding one more twist to an already unusual laureateship.

title: "Murder Most Foul" released
text: In March 2020, early in the pandemic, he released a seventeen-minute song about the Kennedy assassination without warning, his first new original song in eight years.
long: He posted the song at midnight with a short note thanking fans and wishing them safety, and it arrived as many people were first sheltering at home. Built on soft piano, violin and light percussion, it unfolds slowly over seventeen minutes, its spoken-sung verses moving from the shooting in Dallas into a long roll call of songs, films and performers from American culture. Nothing like it had come from him in years, and it drew enormous attention and praise. Two more new songs followed in the next weeks, and in June he released Rough and Rowdy Ways, his first album of original songs since Tempest in 2012. The long track filled a disc of its own as the album's closer, and the record was greeted as one of his strongest late works.

title: Song catalog sold
text: In December 2020 he sold the rights to his entire songwriting catalog to Universal Music Publishing Group.
long: The deal covered his rights in more than six hundred songs, written across six decades, from his earliest records to his newest. No official price was announced, though it was widely reported to be in the hundreds of millions of dollars. The sale was among the largest of a wave of catalog deals in those years, as investors and publishers paid record sums for the songwriting rights of veteran artists, and it drew attention partly because Dylan had long been seen as fiercely protective of his work. Universal gained control of licensing the songs for films, advertisements and cover versions. About a year later he made a separate agreement selling the rights to his recorded music to Sony, which had long released his albums through Columbia.

title: Shadow Kingdom stream
text: In July 2021 he presented Shadow Kingdom, a filmed concert of reworked older songs streamed online.
long: With live concerts halted by the pandemic, he made a film instead of a tour. Directed by Alma Har'el and shot in black and white, it placed him in a smoky, imagined nightclub, with a small band of masked musicians and an audience of extras who drank and smoked at tables. Most of the songs came from the 1960s and 1970s, slowed down, rearranged and sung in the rough, close voice of his later years, so that familiar material sounded freshly made. The event was sold as a paid online stream and surprised viewers who had expected an ordinary concert film. Later it emerged that the music on the soundtrack had been played by different musicians than those on screen. A soundtrack album appeared in 2023, and by late 2021 he was back on the road.

title: The Philosophy of Modern Song
text: He published a book of essays on dozens of songs by other artists, his first book of new prose since Chronicles: Volume One in 2004.
long: The book collects short pieces on songs recorded by other people, ranging across early country and blues, rock and roll, pop standards and punk. Each essay usually takes two forms at once: a loose, second-person riff that imagines its way inside the song, followed by a more direct reflection on the record, the performer or the world around it. The pages are packed with photographs and pictures drawn from popular culture. Critics found it erratic, funny, opinionated and often brilliant, a portrait of his tastes as much as of the songs themselves. Its release had one embarrassment: buyers of expensive signed copies discovered the signatures had been made by machine, and the publisher and Dylan apologized and offered refunds.
